content: Refractive amblyopia is a prevalent condition in childhood that leads to reduced visual acuity, but the most effective treatment approach remains unclear. This review analyzed the effects of treatment using spectacles and conventional occlusion therapy. The objective of the review was to evaluate the effectiveness of spectacles, occlusion therapy, or a combination of both in treating unilateral and bilateral refractive amblyopia. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, mRCT, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, was conducted. The search included studies published up to January 24, 2012, without restrictions on date or language. Relevant conference proceedings were also manually reviewed. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving treatment of unilateral or bilateral refractive amblyopia with spectacles, with or without occlusion, were included. Participants of any age were eligible. Two independent reviewers assessed the abstracts, obtained full-text articles, and contacted study authors when necessary. Eleven trials met the inclusion criteria, but data extraction was only possible for eight of them. No trials included participants with bilateral amblyopia. Due to the limited number of trials for each outcome, no meta-analysis was performed. The included studies primarily focused on unilateral refractive amblyopia. One trial compared three groups: spectacles only versus no treatment, spectacles plus occlusion versus no treatment, and spectacles plus occlusion versus spectacles only. For the spectacles-only group compared to no treatment, the mean visual acuity in the amblyopic eye was 0.31 (SD 0.17) versus 0.42 (SD 0.19), with a mean difference (MD) of -0.11 (borderline statistical significance; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.22 to 0.00). For the spectacles plus occlusion group compared to no treatment, the mean visual acuity was 0.22 (SD 0.13) versus 0.42 (SD 0.19), with an MD of -0.20 (statistically significant; 95% CI -0.30 to -0.10). When comparing spectacles plus occlusion to spectacles only, the MD was -0.09 (borderline statistical significance; 95% CI -0.18 to 0.00). Two additional trials examining this comparison reported MDs of -0.15 (not statistically significant; 95% CI -0.32 to 0.02) and 0.01 (not statistically significant; 95% CI -0.08 to 0.10), respectively. Three trials investigated different occlusion regimens. One trial compared two hours versus six hours of occlusion for moderate amblyopia, reporting an MD of 0.01 (not statistically significant; 95% CI -0.06 to 0.08). Another trial compared six hours versus full-time occlusion for severe amblyopia, with an MD of 0.03 (not statistically significant; 95% CI -0.08 to 0.14). A third trial also compared six hours versus full-time occlusion, reporting an MD of -0.12 (not statistically significant; 95% CI -0.27 to 0.03). One trial evaluated occlusion supplemented with near or distance activities, reporting an MD of -0.03 (not statistically significant; 95% CI -0.09 to 0.03). Another trial compared partial occlusion combined with glasses to glasses alone, with an MD of -0.01 (not statistically significant; 95% CI -0.05 to 0.03). The authors concluded that in some cases of unilateral refractive amblyopia, refractive correction alone provides a treatment benefit. When amblyopia persists, adding occlusion therapy can further improve visual outcomes. However, despite advancements in understanding amblyopia treatment, individualized treatment plans remain challenging to develop. The dose-response relationship of occlusion therapy requires further clarification. Additionally, partial occlusion appears to have a similar effect to glasses alone when initiated simultaneously for unilateral refractive amblyopia. Further research is needed to explore treatment regimens for both unilateral and bilateral refractive amblyopia.
